version.note: The Elgar Society identifies this as Elgar’s first complete recording of the march, distinguishing it from the severely cut 1914 acoustic version. Complete does not establish that every written repeat was taken. The precise performing edition and organ participation are not established.

performers.note: The label explicitly says conducted by Sir Edward Elgar; the composer credit alone was not used to infer this role.

date.note: Independently documented in the Elgar Society recording account and Naxos 8.111022 discography. Internet Archive’s date 1927 concerns the Victor issue, not the recording session. The identifier retains that issue year.

place.note: Venue is printed on the disc label; it is not inferred from the orchestra’s Royal Albert Hall name.

label.note: The label says Orthophonic Recording, identifying the electrical process.

catalogue.note: Victor 9016 couples Marches Nos. 1 and 2; the January 1927 trade listing identifies the same performers.

matrixTakeSides.note: The specialist Naxos discography lists matrix CR 336-2 and original British issue HMV D 1102. The transferred pressing’s take suffix is not independently legible. Internet Archive’s matrix 9016A is the issue-side number, and its other ID CR331 is not silently adopted as the master number.

composition.value: Elgar’s original 1901 march is public domain in ordinary life-plus-70 jurisdictions
composition.note: Elgar died in 1934. This concerns the underlying composition, not an unidentified modern edition.

recording.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: Victor 9016 announced for publication on 28 January 1927
recording.note: Rule 3. The Talking Machine World, 15 January 1927, p. 131, lists 9016 under the Victor list for 28 January, naming both marches and Elgar with the Royal Albert Hall Orchestra. This is publication evidence, not a session-date substitution; the British first issue may be earlier. Its 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established. The selected Great 78 item, original FLAC and label were checked; no NC licence or separate upstream digital recording is stated. The Naxos booklet is used only as documentary evidence: its commercial restoration is not the selected audio.
